title: Perioral (periorificial) dermatitis
summary: Small red papules and pustules around the mouth, nose or eyes with a clear rim next to the lips, often provoked by topical or inhaled steroids and heavy creams. Stop the steroid, expect a rebound, and treat with topical metronidazole or azelaic acid, or an oral tetracycline.

what: **Perioral dermatitis** (periorificial dermatitis) is a common facial eruption of small papules and pustules around the mouth, nose and sometimes eyes, with a characteristic **clear zone next to the lip vermilion**. It mainly affects women aged 20–45 and children.

list: **Topical corticosteroids** on the face are the commonest trigger; also inhaled or nasal steroids, and heavy moisturisers or foundations.
Fluorinated toothpaste and barrier disruption may contribute.
Monomorphic 1–2 mm red papules, papulovesicles and pustules on a red, sometimes scaly background.
Around the mouth, nasolabial folds, chin; may involve the sides of the nose and eyelids (**periocular**).
**Vermilion sparing**: a narrow clear rim around the lips.
Burning or tightness more than itch; no comedones.

diagnosis: Clinical. Ask specifically about steroid creams, inhalers, nasal sprays and cosmetics.

head: Look-alike
Clues
rows: Older; flushing; central face; no clear perioral rim
Greasy scale in nasolabial folds and brows
Itch, eczematous, linked to a product

list: **Stop the facial steroid** (taper systemic or high-potency use with the prescriber; never stop inhaled asthma steroids: rinse and wipe the face after use).
Warn of a **rebound flare** for 1–2 weeks after stopping.
‘Zero therapy’: stop all creams and cosmetics; use a gentle cleanser only.
Oral tetracycline for 6–8 weeks if needed (erythromycin if under 12).

red_flags: Granulomatous or periocular disease not responding, or diagnostic doubt: dermatology.
pearls: Pharmacists often spot inhaled-steroid perioral dermatitis: advise rinsing and wiping the face after inhalers.
Hydrocortisone makes it look better briefly, then worse.
